labels.name: (unnamed) : The band's record label sought to promote them in a similar direction to the Beastie Boys, influencing their crossover appeal.

podcast.title: Alternative Club and Radio Presence
podcast.body: House of Pain's music was increasingly heard in alternative dance clubs and on new rock radio stations, indicating its growing crossover appeal. "Meanwhile, groups like House of Pain and Cypress Hill and Body Count were heard more and more in alternative dance clubs and on new rock radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Crossover Appeal Factors
podcast.body: The band's success in crossing over into the alternative universe may have been influenced by the fact that its core members were white, similar to the Beastie Boys, and that their record label actively pushed them in that direction. "Maybe it had something to do with the fact that its core members were white, like the Beastie Boys, and that their record label wanted to push them in the same direction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Member Success
podcast.body: After House of Pain broke up, two members achieved further fame independently: Everlast and DJ Lethal, who went on to join Limp Bizkit. "After they broke up, two members would find more fame on their own. There was Everlast, and then there's DJ Lethal, who landed up with Limp Biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

concerts.title: Judgment Night (1993) Soundtrack Collaboration
concerts.body: House of Pain went into the studio with Helmets for the soundtrack of the 1993 movie "Judgment Night," producing a "big alternative club hit." "Helmets, together with House of Pain and a big alternative club hit from 1993."

concerts.title: Lollapalooza Years Inclusiveness
concerts.body: House of Pain, originating from LA in the early 90s, was "swept into the inclusiveness" that characterized the original Lollapalooza years, benefiting from the festival's diverse bookings. "House of Pain came out of LA in the early 90s and were swept into the inclusiveness that came during the original Lollapalooze years."
